utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Case number IT-95-14/2-T, The Prosector versus Dario Kordic and Mario Cerkez.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I would first like to ask the usher to put in front of the witness the Croatian translation of his earlier statements which he had on the table yesterday. If I may, just for the record, note that there are two omissions in transcripts. It was on the page 72, line 25, but the words "Gardiska Brigada" were omitted, and on page 105, line 17, the witness there said that he was talking with area commander. The word "area" is omitted. And then if I may continue. [Interpretation] Mr. Breljas, good morning.

utterances.speaker: ANTE BRELJAS [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: At the closing of the session yesterday we talked about your appointment to the post of the IPD officer. With regard to that, if you could just additionally tell us whether anybody explained to you the duties of an IPD officer based on the organisation of that time.

utterances.speaker: ANTE BRELJAS [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Sir, nobody needed -- nobody could actually explain anything to me. I was explaining things to them. I knew, and they didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Given the role of Marinko Plavcic, who in fact carried out the duties of the IPD assistant commander for the Vitezovi, you were formally deputy?

utterances.speaker: ANTE BRELJAS [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes, I was, until Mr. Stewart at one point came with a group of journalists for some kind of control, and I asked him whether these journalists came with him. He said they did not. Then I rounded up the journalists and asked them who they were. I told them that they could not work there, take any pictures, until they received any permission from the competent authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Mr. Breljas, we would gladly hear you out, but let's leave it alone. When were you promoted to the assistant for IPD?

utterances.speaker: ANTE BRELJAS [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Ten, twelve days after all of this, after Ahmici.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So can we say in early May?

utterances.speaker: ANTE BRELJAS [RESUMED]
utterances.text: No. Well, let's say that it was the second half of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well, thank you. So now you had an operative relation to the officer in the headquarters or, as you call it, the military district at a higher level. How do you mean at a higher level?

utterances.speaker: ANTE BRELJAS [RESUMED]
utterances.text: I worked with the IPD officer at the Central Bosnia operative zone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Who was this officer for IPD at the Central Bosnia operative zone?

utterances.speaker: ANTE BRELJAS [RESUMED]
utterances.text: I started this much later because nobody had explained to me what the duties were. I knew what the duties were, but I did not know where to go. So I cannot recall the name of this IPD officer. I believe that he was a veterinarian or something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Mr. Breljas, would it refresh your mind if I said that at first it was Mario Prskalo?

utterances.speaker: ANTE BRELJAS [RESUMED]
utterances.text: No, it was not Mario Prskalo. But this was not Mario Prskalo; this was somebody else.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Let's just try to clear up this matter, because this may become useful later on. Mario Prskalo was the person who was injured by a sniper coming out of the war area on the 17th of April?

utterances.speaker: ANTE BRELJAS [RESUMED]
utterances.text: I did not hear of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: How about Mario Ramljak?

utterances.speaker: ANTE BRELJAS [RESUMED]
utterances.text: I don't think that I should meddle in names. I am bad with names. I know faces.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well. That is an answer too. Is it true that not very regularly, but approximately once a week, the IPD meetings at the operative zone took place?

utterances.speaker: ANTE BRELJAS [RESUMED]
utterances.text: That is not true. It was once a week. I'm confused about the dates, but it was Wednesday or Friday, because I confused them with the press conferences.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So it was as often as once a week?

utterances.speaker: ANTE BRELJAS [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes, it was once a week, and once a month you had to have a report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kovacic, in your exchange with the witness, please make a pause. And I address myself to the witness as well, to wait a few seconds for the interpretation, because the interpretation is going at such a pace that it is difficult to follow.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Mr. Breljas, this is my fault. We speak the same language and so we respond right away. We need to pause between questions and answers. With regard to these meetings, the chairperson was the IPD officer whose name you cannot recall?

utterances.speaker: ANTE BRELJAS [RESUMED]
utterances.text: I just remember that it was Ramljak.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: As a rule, he was the one who chaired it?

utterances.speaker: ANTE BRELJAS [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes, he conducted -- he led these meetings, because it was his duty.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And IPD officers from within the operative zone also attended?

utterances.speaker: ANTE BRELJAS [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You told us, but it wasn't quite clear, so let us try to clarify this. In your previous statement, and yesterday, you said that the Vitezovi administratively were known as the 4th brigade, and basically for the logistical reasons?

utterances.speaker: ANTE BRELJAS [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes, we -- whatever the operative zone of Vitez had, it was divided into four parts. The Vitezovi formed this fourth part and this is how everything was distributed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: There was no other organisational link between the Vitez Brigade and the Vitezovi?

utterances.speaker: ANTE BRELJAS [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Nothing in terms of orders, but there were contacts.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You mentioned your role when you spoke about the Tuzla convoy?

utterances.speaker: ANTE BRELJAS [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I will also remind you that you mentioned this in your statement, a rather comprehensive statement you gave in 1996, to the Bosnian authorities.

utterances.speaker: ANTE BRELJAS [RESUMED]
utterances.text: That is what I spoke about to the Bosnian authorities. This is what they were mostly interested in.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You have it in front of you from 1996. In the Croatian text this is page 6, paragraph 5, and in the English version it is page 10, paragraph 2. Did you find that?

utterances.speaker: ANTE BRELJAS [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes. I don't need to remind myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So did you look at it?

utterances.speaker: ANTE BRELJAS [RESUMED]
utterances.text: I remember it very well, because it was the -- it is the greatest embarrassment of the Croatian people. Actually, not the Croatian people; they're honest, but it's these bandits who did it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Let me read it to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just a moment. Is this being translated?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: As I said, Your Honour, it is in the English text. It is a statement, previous statement of the witness to the Bosnian authorities, dated 7 November 1996, and in the English text it is on page 10, the very last paragraph, on the bottom of the page. One before last. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: This is the paragraph which reads: "Kraljevic asked me to interpret ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Exactly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The English translations would appear in the text -- in the transcript, if you're going to put something about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Could it be put on the ELMO?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Perhaps it could be put on the ELMO, and you could read it in Croatian and it could be interpreted.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So we see on the ELMO the marked paragraph that I will read in Croatian. Is that correct, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: "Kraljevic asked me to interpret and tell the U.N. soldiers something to the effect that they could not go any further or they would be attacked, or they would be accused falsely of transporting wounded from Stari Vitez, at which they even offered their tanks for inspection. But in spite of this, they were not allowed through. I stayed in Dubravica until 0200 the following morning, barring passage to the UNPROFOR when Kraljevic ordered me, by courier, to let them through." Mr. Breljas, you gave this statement in 1996 when your memory was fresher?

utterances.speaker: ANTE BRELJAS [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: There you never mentioned by a single word Mr. Cerkez, and you mentioned him for the first time in 1998. Could you please tell us what is correct here?

utterances.speaker: ANTE BRELJAS [RESUMED]
utterances.text: What is correct is that I saw Mario Cerkez there when I arrived. He asked me to interpret, and I told him that I did not want to do that because Kraljevic was my commander and he was the only one whom I recognised. When he arrived, then whatever he told me, I interpreted, and I told the Major, the commander of this tank and transporter, everything that was asked of me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So, Mr. Breljas, to sum up, you say that the statements you gave in 1998, in 2000, is more detailed and more correct?

utterances.speaker: ANTE BRELJAS [RESUMED]
utterances.text: No. I just omitted it in the first because I didn't think that it was necessary, because we were just discussing the stopping of this convoy, and I did not think that Mario Cerkez had anything to do with it, whereas there were people who knew more about it, and I knew that this was an institution where I needed to provide more detail so nobody would try to lay any traps for me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Mr. Breljas, you -- at the end of the statement it says that you dictated this statement and that you accept it by placing your signature on it?

utterances.speaker: ANTE BRELJAS [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So, as you mentioned two persons regarding this incident, Darko was the commander?

utterances.speaker: ANTE BRELJAS [RESUMED]
utterances.text: No. Mario was the commander, but I only took orders from Kraljevic. But Mario was the commander of all this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Have you finished with that document?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Yes. I've finished with that document. I will kindly ask the usher to show yesterday presented Exhibit Z1380.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is, again, a comprehensive document. Yesterday, Mr. Breljas, you saw that, and it will be placed in front of you. It is a report of the Vitezovi, addressed to the headquarters of the HVO, HRHB in Mostar. Let me ask you a couple of things in connection with that. Yesterday you did not give a clear answer with respect to who was superior to the Vitezovi, to whom they reported, and I would like you to look at this document. Do you have it in front of you?

utterances.speaker: ANTE BRELJAS [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: First, it is beyond dispute that this is a report of Vitezovi, dated 18 February 1994, addressed to the main headquarter in Mostar.

utterances.speaker: ANTE BRELJAS [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Let me look at this signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Look at the header and look at the signatures.

utterances.speaker: ANTE BRELJAS [RESUMED]
utterances.text: First of all, this is not true. This was written at a time when Mr. Kraljevic was already demoted. They wanted to destroy him. So there are many lies in here. He used irrelevant truthful facts, and he interspersed them among the lies, because he wanted to destroy Darko Kraljevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Excuse me, sir. Is this report sent to the main headquarters in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: ANTE BRELJAS [RESUMED]
utterances.text: I don't know. The only thing I can say, that I handled all the reports and orders sent by Darko Kraljevic, and this was not done by him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: In other words, you do not know, sir.

utterances.speaker: ANTE BRELJAS [RESUMED]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well. Do you agree that Vitezovi were under the command of the HVO -- that is, the main headquarters in Mostar -- or do you not agree with that?

utterances.speaker: ANTE BRELJAS [RESUMED]
utterances.text: For a period of time, until Darko Kraljevic was killed; that is, in early 1993 they came under the command of Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So you agree with that. But they were -- in operative terms, they were under the Central Bosnia operative zone commander?

utterances.speaker: ANTE BRELJAS [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So that was Mr. Blaskic?

utterances.speaker: ANTE BRELJAS [RESUMED]
utterances.text: No. Mr. Blaskic only became commander sometime in July 1993. Until then he was in Vitez, but nobody really followed him and respected his orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So you are saying that Blaskic, in early 1993, did not have an operational control?

utterances.speaker: ANTE BRELJAS [RESUMED]
utterances.text: No, he never did at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So far in these proceedings there was a couple of -- there were a couple of written comments signed by Blaskic in the first half of a year. I am not talking about the later period, from which one we can clearly conclude that those comments are addressed to all subordinate units, and usually and explicitly Vitez unit is listed. So if you want, I can go, I can take a couple of them and show them the witness or we just put it on the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Kovacic, you must take whichever course you think is right. You can make comments, of course, on the documents in due course at an appropriate time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Then I will go for the comments, because I don't think that we should waste the time on the wrong information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness Breljas, yesterday you mentioned taking of the prisoners to dig trenches, in other words, use them for military purposes, and you mentioned specifically two persons. Certain Mile Vinac, do you actually know where he belonged within the HVO organisation?

utterances.speaker: ANTE BRELJAS [RESUMED]
utterances.text: I don't know if he was Mile, but I know that his name was Vinac. Organisationally he belonged to the Vitez Brigade. He was a commander of the labour platoons. He rounded up both civilians and detainees to do different kinds of work in and around Vitez. I don't know his first name, but it was Vinac.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Breljas. If I put it to you that he was part of the civilian administration in Vitez, would you still claim that he -- with certainty that he was a member of the brigade?

utterances.speaker: ANTE BRELJAS [RESUMED]
utterances.text: I do not agree that he was a civilian.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You are sure that he was a member of the brigade?

utterances.speaker: ANTE BRELJAS [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Don't talk about certainty. I know that he did this on behalf of the brigade, and who he was organisationally within the municipality, I don't know. I had enough of Vitezovi to deal with.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Mr. Breljas, perhaps we can clarify this. Nobody expects of you to know everything. You can say, "I am sure" about something, you can say, "I think that this is" or "I don't know," but do you categorically affirm that he was a member of the Viteska Brigade?

utterances.speaker: ANTE BRELJAS [RESUMED]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Yesterday you mentioned the second person whom you linked to the Vitez Brigade. His nickname was Zabac or Frog; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANTE BRELJAS [RESUMED]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Without going through all these statements, in no statements previously, either in one in '96 or the one in 1998, did you mention his name?

utterances.speaker: ANTE BRELJAS [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Look, there was a dilemma here. I don't know whether Zabac was a member of the Kaonik Camp or a commander of the police of the Vitez Brigade. This is my dilemma. I know both of them. The one in Kaonik was a short man and sort of stocky, and the one in the Vitez Brigade was sort of medium height and thin. And I have confusion over names, which is reflected in my statements. I was an outsider, so I could not place names and faces together. So I don't know who he was, but one of them was Zabac.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Mr. Breljas, if I mention the name Aleksovski to you, do you know who that is; a short one?

utterances.speaker: ANTE BRELJAS [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yeah, right. Then Zabac was the commander of the police and he was in the Vitez Brigade. Then that is all right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And which military police do you mean, the military police or the Vitez Brigade?

utterances.speaker: ANTE BRELJAS [RESUMED]
utterances.text: But the brigade does not have a military police. They have a platoon which is there responsible for the military area. Excuse me, but I know that men called their police and they came, arrested this soldier, and kept him in custody for five days.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Right. Thank you. I should like the witness to be shown Z1335,1 and Z808. Mr. Breljas, it is the two lists of the facilities. One of them is yours on December '93. That one is signed by your colleague Cilic on the 24th of April, '93. You said that some names appeared on both lists. I should merely like to ask you to look at the first list, Cilic's list, which is document Z808, and look at the name in the upper part under 2, "Kolak Lovro," and "Brankov" in brackets. Brankov in brackets is the father's name. That is, I think, how we usually do it; we put the father's name of the soldier in brackets. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANTE BRELJAS [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And then we come across that same name in your list under number 9, "Kolak Lovro," and then in brackets it says "Marko," so that is not the same person. Or perhaps it is a confusion?

utterances.speaker: ANTE BRELJAS [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Excuse me, sir. Listen to me. In Vitez there are only three or four surnames, so whether he is Marko or Marko, it is really very difficult to clarify that. But be that as it may, my list is the list of men killed in PPN Vitezovi, but when the Vitez Brigade, somebody else started sending in their males into Vitezovi, he was sent to Vitezovi and he was killed with the Vitezovi, and that is how I filed him. And then at the end, when I took it to the military district, I realised then that he'd also been on the roster of the Vitez Brigade. So, you know, I mean, he was killed when Vitezovi -- and if the Vitez Brigade also put him on his list, on this list, then I can do nothing about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Right. But from what you said, I gather two things: Same first names and surnames are quite frequent?

utterances.speaker: ANTE BRELJAS [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Well, you have Ramljak, for instance. Half of the Vitez military district is Ramljak. And then you have to go into names of fathers, mothers. It's all very difficult.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Yeah, right, but will you please try to answer my questions and then we shall be able to proceed faster. There were also cases when soldiers changed units, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ANTE BRELJAS [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes, but that was towards the end.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So that would conclude that part of my examination. But it reminds me: The list mentions, and you also mentioned yesterday Plavcic, who was killed near Novi Travnik. And I conclude from that that the Vitezovi or, rather, that you are aware that the Vitezovi also operated outside the municipality of Vitez.

utterances.speaker: ANTE BRELJAS [RESUMED]
utterances.text: The Vitezovi, I don't know. I was not there at the time. But the Vitezovi also operated in Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: No, no, no. I mean the Vitezovi which had its seat in Vitez, Kraljevic's.

utterances.speaker: ANTE BRELJAS [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes, I heard about that. I heard that, but I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: But at the time when you were there, there is no doubt that they were also in Novi Travnik?

utterances.speaker: ANTE BRELJAS [RESUMED]
utterances.text: They were -- the farthest they got -- what was that place where the -- where the fire was set afire? Yes, Opara. Opara, that is furthest they got. And then on the other side, Prosje, something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Right. But that is outside the municipality of Vitez?

utterances.speaker: ANTE BRELJAS [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes, it is outside it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You yesterday told us, and it was page 68, about a command of the Vitez Brigade, that the Vitezovi -- according to which Vitezovi were made responsible for catching the deserters or, rather, draft dodgers, and to take them back to the front.

utterances.speaker: ANTE BRELJAS [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes, that is so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Will the witness be shown Z1279. It was on another document produced yesterday. Will the usher please place the English text on the ELMO. And you can turn to page 5, the bottom half of the page.

utterances.speaker: ANTE BRELJAS [RESUMED]
utterances.text: The pages are not marked here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: That's quite true. The Croatian version does not have that. So will you please look at the last page. But you should remind yourself who is writing to whom. So who is this addressed to? Page number 5 of this document, lower part of the page. Last page of the document, usher. I'm sorry, one before that, number 5. Right. And lower part of the page to be -- down, down, down, down. This part. Correct. Fine. So, Mr. Breljas, we could see that this was a document of the Travnik defence administration, and it was a sector in the Ministry of Defence of the HZ-HB; that it was signed by the head of the administration, Anto Puljic. And on the last page I'd asked you to look at, will you please look at item 4. It says: "Owing to inefficient mobilisation, an order was issued to the military police which brought people to the front line but was inefficient because the military conscripts abandoned positions without permission and came back." Then in 5 it says: "The Vitezovi special purpose unit was successful in carrying out its orders and brought all the military conscripts to the front line. After this, unfit military conscripts were released from military service completely or engaged elsewhere." So it is quite obvious that some authorised body issued a written order to this effect to the Vitezovi?

utterances.speaker: ANTE BRELJAS [RESUMED]
utterances.text: That is not true, because such a written order could have been issued only to me, or if they bypassed me wrongfully and then reached someone else. Whatever was done, illegally, unlawfully, I know nothing about that. I was -- had nothing to do with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: But you said that the Vitez Brigade gave such an order to the Vitezovi, and before that you also said that Cerkez had issued -- had Cerkez issued an order to the Vitezovi, they would have killed him.

utterances.speaker: ANTE BRELJAS [RESUMED]
utterances.text: I don't understand you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: That is what you said yesterday. You are affirming that the Vitez Brigade asked the Vitezovi to capture the draft dodgers?

utterances.speaker: ANTE BRELJAS [RESUMED]
utterances.text: No. That is not what I said, sir. All I said was that the name of the Vitezovi was to be marred. And when people were fleeing, they were trying to make Vitezovi go round the houses and thus tarnish the image among the civilian population, that they were the ones that were rounding up people and taking them to the front.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I see. So you are not claiming that they were doing that on the orders of the Vitez Brigade?

utterances.speaker: ANTE BRELJAS [RESUMED]
utterances.text: No, I'm not, because I'm also claiming that it did not come from Novi Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Right. Now some minor things. Excuse me, Mr. Breljas. I'm sorry. We can do this very quickly. Yesterday you said certain things, and we agreed that the Vitezovi Brigade was in the elementary school in Dubravica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kovacic, I should like to ask the witness, Mr. Breljas, who is it that wanted to tarnish the image of the Vitezovi? You said that somebody was trying to tarnish the image of the Vitezovi among the civilian population. Who was that?

utterances.speaker: ANTE BRELJAS [RESUMED]
utterances.text: The HVO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Why do you say that? Why do you think that?

utterances.speaker: ANTE BRELJAS [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Because the Vitezovi enjoyed a major reputation, and even today they are very famous. Yes, they were perhaps slightly aggressive, actually at some times rough, but they were the best soldiers in that area. So when the HVO was taking over the command from the HOS, they could not destroy that name, the name of Vitezovi, and they had to first to raise it as high as they could so as to bring it down as much. So that they brought in moles to destroy that unit from inside, such as Vinac and other people, and there were quite a number of other people who were working in order to damage the representation of Vitezovi.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So in your mind, it is the HVO which conducted this operation to tarnish the image of the Vitezovi?

utterances.speaker: ANTE BRELJAS [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes. That is correct. And to break down that unit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: If I may continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A place near Dubravica where people gathered regularly, an alternate military district command post, was in Kolonija, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: ANTE BRELJAS [RESUMED]
utterances.text: That was before me, and after that it was across the street from Vinac, in that other part where the school was later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: But that is the same block of buildings, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ANTE BRELJAS [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So the two of us know it. But a block is a block of buildings within the town of Vitez?

utterances.speaker: ANTE BRELJAS [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes. That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Now, another thing. Darko Kraljevic lived in Rijeka, in the immediate vicinity of the military station and Sumarija?

utterances.speaker: ANTE BRELJAS [RESUMED]
utterances.text: That's where his house was, but he also had a flat in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Yes, but he had a house up there and his mother lived there?

utterances.speaker: ANTE BRELJAS [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes, that is quite true.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And his fellows, his men, all gathered there and guarded the house?

utterances.speaker: ANTE BRELJAS [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes. There were some Vitezovi who were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So we could say, tentatively, that those were three principal places, the points where the Vitezovi gathered and communicated?

utterances.speaker: ANTE BRELJAS [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes, that is quite correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Now, in view of the beginning of this story -- you couldn't remember the date exactly. I'm referring to the 15th and the 16th -- you said that you associated things with events. Now, would you perhaps remember if on one of those days or, more specifically, on the 13th of April, 1993, an attempt was made against Darko Kraljevic's life in Kruscica? Subsequently the information arrived that an attempt had been by Neso Hurem, as the local MOS. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: ANTE BRELJAS [RESUMED]
utterances.text: I was not there at the time, but I remember it. I wasn't there, and I can't really talk about it, because I do not doubt details. Kraljevic would not let people even talk about it later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So it was before you arrived?

utterances.speaker: ANTE BRELJAS [RESUMED]
utterances.text: No. It was while I was in Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Right. Thank you. You spoke about lighting candles, paying homage to the dead on the 1st of November, 1993, and you said that on behalf of the brigade, it was Cerkez who came to light a candle. That is correct?

utterances.speaker: ANTE BRELJAS [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes, it is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So could you please tell us first the day of the dead, the All Souls Day in our parts and in Bosnia and throughout Yugoslavia but especially in Bosnia. That was a very important day, a tradition, and it was always marked? Isn't it true?

utterances.speaker: ANTE BRELJAS [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And is that why you organised it, as an IPD officer?

utterances.speaker: ANTE BRELJAS [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And a priest also came, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: ANTE BRELJAS [RESUMED]
utterances.text: A priest did say that he would come, and I was there waiting for him until half past 1.00. And then I went to have my lunch, but he wasn't turning up, wasn't turning up, and then I grew hungry and I left. And I left Miskovic's assistant there. So she was there, and I went to have my lunch, and it was during that period of time that a priest came or, rather, not a priest but a friar.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Right. But that was not the only place in the Lasva Valley where homage was paid to the victims.

utterances.speaker: ANTE BRELJAS [RESUMED]
utterances.text: No, no, no. That was not the only place. It was all practically the width and breadth of the valley. But there were snipers and it was hazardous, it was dangerous, and people were trying to find some shelter where they would conduct the ceremony.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And I suppose that you know that Cerkez came to the place from another place like that, and then went on to a third place?

utterances.speaker: ANTE BRELJAS [RESUMED]
utterances.text: I wouldn't really know, but I do believe that that is how it was, because yes, he went to those places. That is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And tell us, do you remember if Cerkez was wearing a black jacket on such an occasion? On that occasion. Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: ANTE BRELJAS [RESUMED]
utterances.text: I think that he was wearing a camouflage uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: But isn't it -- shouldn't it -- isn't the black -- aren't black clothes prescribed when you go to the cemetery on such occasions? At least, I mean military black clothes.

utterances.speaker: ANTE BRELJAS [RESUMED]
utterances.text: I don't really want to insist on it, but I do think he was wearing camouflage clothes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Right. Thank you. From your statements, it was said that you agree that the only common higher superior officer to Darko Kraljevic and Mario Cerkez was Mr. Blaskic.

utterances.speaker: ANTE BRELJAS [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Listen. Mr. Blaskic held that post, but nobody obeyed him, and nobody complied with his orders until mid-1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Right. But perhaps there was another person who was their superior, superior to both of them?

utterances.speaker: ANTE BRELJAS [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes. That was Mr. Dario Kordic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You don't have any documents about that or something like that?

utterances.speaker: ANTE BRELJAS [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Naturally, I don't, because he never gave anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So it would be just your estimate?

utterances.speaker: ANTE BRELJAS [RESUMED]
utterances.text: No. This is not an estimate. This is a knowledge. This is an awareness that I have, but I have no proof.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Right. I will not show you an order issued by Blaskic. We can let it be. But, Mr. Breljas, one minor thing: Mr. Breljas, you told us about the strength of Vitezovi, and in the end I should like to ask you what is true and what is not. It seems to me that something was omitted, though not deliberately, but you will tell us. In your statement to the Prosecution in 1998, that is the statement some 30 pages long, and you can look at page 15 of the statement, you said that at that time, at the beginning of the war, Vitezovi were some 367 men strong, and we have it written out. So perhaps I should show it all to you, and you will tell us what is true, what is not. The English text, page 15. Then you say here --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Kovacic, I'm finding this difficult to follow.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And you're also going rather fast, if I may say so. Could you slow down a bit?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Certainly. Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The statement that you made to the Prosecution in 1998. In the Croatian text it is page 13. In the English text it is page 15. And you said that there were 367 Vitezovi in the beginning when you arrived, and that figure is written out in words. Then yesterday you said that there were 180 of them, sometime early during your testimony yesterday. And the third figure is in the summary which the Prosecution prepared for your testimony of the 7th December 1999, and that is you signed every page, and item 5 says that the number was around 350. Then you mention 180 of those who were in Dubravica. Could you please tell us, at long last, which one of these figures is correct?

utterances.speaker: ANTE BRELJAS [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Sir, nobody knows that. Not even Darko Kraljevic would have the exact number. When I refer to 360 Vitezovi, I'm talking about those who are on record and who are on Vitezovi rosters. When I came to Posusje, I had about 400 Vitezovi on the payroll. Then I personally, and I was in the barracks all the time, I knew that there were never more than 180 of them in the barracks; that is, I know of 180 Vitezovi. And all the other figures about the payrolls, those who were at home, those who were there on these lists in order to hide from other units of the Vitezovi, I don't know them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Right. So at least we've clarified this. And may I ask you, then, what does this mean? Because in the next -- in the sentence it says that in addition to a certain number of those who were members of Vitezovi secretly. What does that mean?

utterances.speaker: ANTE BRELJAS [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Well, there were several scouts in Vitezovi about whom nobody knew anything. And there were some people illegally; that is, there were some who operated illegally. Nobody knew about them either, even Blaskic or Darko Kraljevic's superiors. Those were Vitezovi who worked directly for Darko Kraljevic, until he saw that everything was going wrong, that they were beginning to drink and things like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: But you don't know how many of them were there, roughly?

utterances.speaker: ANTE BRELJAS [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes, I could give you the number, but I won't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I would like if you could put on the table in front of the witness the document we saw yesterday, Z1153.1. Mr. Breljas, you have the Croatian version of the document. Can you see the Croatian version? Put the English text on the ELMO. Beginning the first page. Mr. Breljas, we saw this document yesterday. Again, it is the Travnik Defence Administration, Mr. Puljic writing to the head of the Defence for Vitez, Mr. Marijan Skopljak. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANTE BRELJAS [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And we see here a certain number of people, eight to be specific, who were working on Vitez television at the time, are now being assigned to the Vitez Brigade; in other words, mobilised. The question is the following: Do you know anything about the composition of work platoons and the labour obligation that existed at the time?

utterances.speaker: ANTE BRELJAS [RESUMED]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Isn't it clear that this is what the document is about: They were employed in the television, but as of the 3rd of August, the need for troops increased, the situation was becoming difficult, and certain services that were not of vital significance were being mobilised and sent to join the army?

utterances.speaker: ANTE BRELJAS [RESUMED]
utterances.text: No, that is not quite right. There was Zildum, who was an honest person, a journalist, and who couldn't get on with these other thieves, and he was sent to command a reserve unit. But those who were obedient, they stayed on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: But a list is attached to this document with some remarks, an attached page, attached paper. And a matter at the bottom -- at the bottom of the document is clear. A little bit higher, please. Okay. Fine. Mr. Breljas, in the top part you have an indication by hand, and then again for all of them it says, by hand, "all to the front." So one can infer from this that people who were working in the television station were assigned to various military posts, they were mobilised?

utterances.speaker: ANTE BRELJAS [RESUMED]
utterances.text: You are asking me things that I was not interested in, then or now. What did I care about these? I was concerned with the Vitezovi, and I can tell you everything about them, but not about these people. I really had no knowledge about them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: But yesterday you mentioned a cameraman from television as a brigade cameraman?

utterances.speaker: ANTE BRELJAS [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes. He was either a soldier or a TV cameraman. I didn't call him a brigade cameraman. I just said that a cameraman arrived whom I didn't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So you don't know whether he belonged to the brigade or not?

utterances.speaker: ANTE BRELJAS [RESUMED]
utterances.text: How could I know?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In point 23 of this summary you said, and repeated yesterday, that Cerkez and Kraljevic were schoolmates and that they knew each other well, and you based their cooperation on that fact.

utterances.speaker: ANTE BRELJAS [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Well, they knew each other, they came from the same village, they belonged to respected families, and it was normal that they knew each other well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you a few simple questions. Do you know the age difference between the two of them?

utterances.speaker: ANTE BRELJAS [RESUMED]
utterances.text: I don't know how old Mario Cerkez is. I know that Darko was 27.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So the age difference is six years?

utterances.speaker: ANTE BRELJAS [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Very well. Six years.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So then it is to be assumed that they didn't go to school together?

utterances.speaker: ANTE BRELJAS [RESUMED]
utterances.text: I didn't say they went to the same form, but I, as a child, and you, and all of us, some went to 8th grade, others to 1st grade, in the same school, in the same environment. Whether they went to the same school or not, I really don't know. But I know that they were good acquaintances.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let's move on from this point about the school. The witness said yesterday that he wasn't sure about the school.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On several occasions you mentioned a person called Vlado Krizanac as a member of the Vitezovi. Is this the one that was nicknamed Sidi?

utterances.speaker: ANTE BRELJAS [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: But he lived in Krizancevo Selo; you know that?

utterances.speaker: ANTE BRELJAS [RESUMED]
utterances.text: His house was there, but later on he moved into an apartment in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So at the time of the outbreak of the conflict, the 16th of April, he was in Krizancevo Selo? That is only a couple of hundred metres from your headquarters in Dubravica?

utterances.speaker: ANTE BRELJAS [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Let's say 500 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Not more than one kilometre.

utterances.speaker: ANTE BRELJAS [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes, one kilometre on the outside.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Do you know that he was in Dubravica on the 16th of April, in the headquarters, in the barracks, in the school, or was he on the front?

utterances.speaker: ANTE BRELJAS [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes, he was in the base in the school, because Marinko Plavcic was at the gas station; this was in the school. Vinac was --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is what you said earlier on in your statement, but not in your testimony yesterday.

utterances.speaker: ANTE BRELJAS [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, he was in the school.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So to speed things up -- two pictures earlier given as the evidence. Perhaps the witness could help us with them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. If they could be shown to the witness and put on the ELMO too.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Z21774 and Z2773.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: These photographs were tendered with the witness Lee Whitworth. Witness, these are members of the Vitez Brigade. Can you recognise any of the persons on this photograph?

utterances.speaker: ANTE BRELJAS [RESUMED]
utterances.text: No. The one in the middle is Ante Tikvic. He is not a member of the Vitez Brigade but of the Special Purposes Unit, Vitezovi.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Yes, I apologise. I meant members of Vitezovi. You know Ante Tikvic?

utterances.speaker: ANTE BRELJAS [RESUMED]
utterances.text: I know this one too, the one to the right. And that one over there, that you can see only one eye of, looks like Vinac to me, but I am not quite sure. Oh, yes. And this one, of course, this is Niko Krizanac. Of course I know him. And the one holding a rifle, that is Niko Krizanac.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And the one to the left, is that Jako Krizanac?

utterances.speaker: ANTE BRELJAS [RESUMED]
utterances.text: With his back turned. Wait a minute. Wait a minute. I recognise him. That is Niko, Jako, Vinac and Ante Tikvic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: We can see clearly the patch on his uniform that you described to us, but it is also clear from this photograph that this patch does not correspond to either of the two that we saw yesterday. They were the patches under Z1530 and Z2790.

utterances.speaker: ANTE BRELJAS [RESUMED]
utterances.text: This is the Croatian coat of arms, I think, slightly distorted, the Ustashas coat of arms with a white background. It begins with three and four, and then it gets wider and wider.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: But to speed things up, we agree that the Vitezovi wore various patches, a wide variety?

utterances.speaker: ANTE BRELJAS [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So, therefore, not only the two that were shown yesterday?

utterances.speaker: ANTE BRELJAS [RESUMED]
utterances.text: The official was the PPN Vitezovi with a Croatian coat of arms, but the people wore what they wanted.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So can the witness be shown the second photograph, please. So here. Can you recognise any of these?

utterances.speaker: ANTE BRELJAS [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Ante Tikvic is the first. Ante Tikvic from Cajdras. I know this one too.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Which one?

utterances.speaker: ANTE BRELJAS [RESUMED]
utterances.text: The one next to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ANTE BRELJAS [RESUMED]
utterances.text: I can't recognise this one. And the one at the end is familiar.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Is he the Krizanac from the previous photograph with his back turned?

utterances.speaker: ANTE BRELJAS [RESUMED]
utterances.text: If that is him, then it is not Jako Krizanac. In this photograph it looks like Jako Krizanac to me, but here I am not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Anyway, these that you have recognised are Vitezovi members?

utterances.speaker: ANTE BRELJAS [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes, the first two. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. My last area would be to ask you to identify for me some names, if you can recollect them, members of Vitezovi. They are the names, most of which have been mentioned in this case, but we are not sure which unit they belong to. Dragan Vinac, you said he was a member of the Vitezovi?

utterances.speaker: ANTE BRELJAS [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes. That is where the HVO started and that is when he joined.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: But there is a Dragan Vinac from Donji Veceriska?

utterances.speaker: ANTE BRELJAS [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes, I heard about him. But that's the problem, you see. You have so many people with the same surnames.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: No, Dragan Vinac from Donji Veceriska, I think that is one and the same man. Some others from Donji Veceriska that I should like to mention that were referred to indirectly: Josip Franjic, known as Jesus, or Jesus, do you remember him, rapidly?

utterances.speaker: ANTE BRELJAS [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Now, wait a minute. I have to think about it. I can't answer just like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I apologise. I am just saying that you don't have to give explanations; just try and remember, if you can.

utterances.speaker: ANTE BRELJAS [RESUMED]
utterances.text: No, I'm afraid I can't recollect.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: What about Zoran Franjic?

utterances.speaker: ANTE BRELJAS [RESUMED]
utterances.text: That sounds familiar.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Franjo Sapina?

utterances.speaker: ANTE BRELJAS [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes, I know him. He was Kraljevic's deputy in the first period, wasn't he? No. No. He was a soldier.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: In the Vitezovi. All these are Vitezovi, aren't they? Darko Drmic?

utterances.speaker: ANTE BRELJAS [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes, he's Plavcic's son-in-law, or vice versa; I'm not sure. No, he is Plavcic's son-in-law or brother-in-law.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: From Donji Veceriska?

utterances.speaker: ANTE BRELJAS [RESUMED]
utterances.text: No, from Dubravica.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Fine. And Zoran Franjic, known as Goran?

utterances.speaker: ANTE BRELJAS [RESUMED]
utterances.text: I don't know where he is from.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You don't know him. Very well. You mentioned him in an earlier statement as a lieutenant, as a logistics officer?

utterances.speaker: ANTE BRELJAS [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Whom?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Zoran Franjic.

utterances.speaker: ANTE BRELJAS [RESUMED]
utterances.text: No. I mentioned Buha.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: No, wait a minute. Wait a minute. On page 14 of your statement.

utterances.speaker: ANTE BRELJAS [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Let me try and remember. Where is that list? Alilovic was the logistics man. Alilovic, not Franjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I also have information that Marko Prskalo was with you, working with you.

utterances.speaker: ANTE BRELJAS [RESUMED]
utterances.text: He wasn't in Vitezovi at all. There was Stipa Batalja [phoen], who was in charge of the warehouse, Jozo Buha.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Witness Breljas, will you look at page 14 of the Croatian version of your statement where you mentioned names of members of the command. You mentioned Zoran Franjic, lieutenant, logistics officer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just one moment. Page 15 of the English, and it should be put on the ELMO so that we can all see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I suppose so. You can use mine if you want.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, please look at page 14, where you see the list.

utterances.speaker: ANTE BRELJAS [RESUMED]
utterances.text: It's all right. I can read from the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You start listing the people: Kraljevic, Vinac, Sapina, Plavcic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It may be that this is important at some stage in the trial. It may be simplest, Mr. Kovacic, if you read out the list and so it's in evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You listed as members of the command: Darko Kraljevic, Dragan Vinac, Berislav Sapina, Marinko Plavcic, Dragan Markovic, Zoran Franjic, Ivica Alilovic, and your own name, Anto Breljas. That is what you told the investigator. Is that what you still believe?

utterances.speaker: ANTE BRELJAS [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes. I didn't mention Dragan Markovic and Zoran Franjic. Miso Mijic is at the end and actually he was always number 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Miso Mijic has not been read out. Something that I have in my notes. Mr. Breljas, one more question for you, which I have been prompted to ask by the question by His Honour, the Judge. You mentioned that you had a personal conflict with Dragan Vinac, the assistant commander. Why?

utterances.speaker: ANTE BRELJAS [RESUMED]
utterances.text: I never was in conflict with him. However, I saw that Dragan Vinac does not belong to the Vitezovi, that he was only provoking problems and listing the Vitezovi as thugs. There were very good guys in the Vitezovi, very brave fighters, but he socialised with all those who were looting, killing and causing trouble. And I said to Darko Kraljevic, you know, "Dragan Vinac somehow doesn't fit." And he said, "What are you talking about?" But in fact he had taken over command from Darko Kraljevic, and later on I established why and how and whom he belonged to, and this would lead me to much higher echelons which would have far more serious consequences for me and for people at much higher positions, so I wouldn't like to go into it. I have evidence that Dragan Vinac wanted to destroy the Vitezovi, and he did do that and he collaborated with Mario Cerkez and with Kordic. And later on, when he saw that Blaskic had taken over power, he joined Blaskic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So all this was your own assessment and you conveyed your impressions to Darko Kraljevic. Thank you. I have no further questions for this witness, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I have a few points of clarification, after this cross-examination. Witness Breljas, you spoke of the meeting which was held in Dubravica between Dario Kordic, Darko Kraljevic, Dragan Vinac, Miso Mijic and another person you no longer recollect. You said that this meeting was held during the night that preceded the attack on Vitez and Ahmici. I am asking you whether you confirm -- you are confirming that that meeting did indeed take place in that night?

utterances.speaker: ANTE BRELJAS [RESUMED]
utterances.text: You see, there is something that both Defence counsel confused me a little. The Defence of Mr. Dario Kordic said that on the 16th I was picked up by Mr. Stewart, that I had spent the night there and things like that. And then Defence counsel of Mario Cerkez said that on the 16th, in Dubravica, Kosina [phoen] pointed his gun at me. However, there is a very small possibility that either Zivko Totic was captured on the 14th or what I said had occurred on the 16th. So there is a very small possibility, which I exclude, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: But please answer my question, Mr. Breljas. That meeting that you spoke about in Dubravica, I am not talking about the date, I am not asking you the name of the day. I am just asking you whether this meeting in Dubravica took place in the night that preceded the attack on Vitez and Ahmici.

utterances.speaker: ANTE BRELJAS [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Whether it was that night or the night after the attack, I am a bit confused, to be quite frank. Was it the first night of the attack or the eve of the attack? I am afraid they have managed to confuse me as to that date. It is quite certain that Mr. Stewart did not spend the night there, that I did not spend the night in any kind of trench. That I can guarantee. I'm quite sure of that. The only thing I'm not quite sure of is whether that was the night after the attack or the night prior to the attack. I'm not quite sure about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: A further point of clarification. When you say that you don't know whether it was the night or the day prior to the attack, do you mean the night between the 15th and the 16th of April or the morning of the 16th of April?

utterances.speaker: ANTE BRELJAS [RESUMED]
utterances.text: The point is that on the next day, the day after that talk, I went to Ahmici. I went to Ahmici. Ahmici had already been destroyed, which means --

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: So that was the day after the meeting?

utterances.speaker: ANTE BRELJAS [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. We have just referred to Miso Mijic who belonged to the secret service, the SIS. Yes. You said that this gentlemen was frequently in contact with your unit commander, Darko Kraljevic. You never said that he was formally a member of the Vitezovi.

utterances.speaker: ANTE BRELJAS [RESUMED]
utterances.text: He was always with Darko. He never separated from him. Darko and he were always together.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Did he wear the insignia of the Vitezovi on his uniform?

utterances.speaker: ANTE BRELJAS [RESUMED]
utterances.text: I'm afraid I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Did you see his name on the Vitezovi lists, registers that you referred to?

utterances.speaker: ANTE BRELJAS [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes. He was on my list as a member of the command. Darko Kraljevic, Miso Mijic. That is why I always thought that Miso Mijic was Darko Kraljevic's assistant. Later on I learned that Darko Kraljevic was his assistant. I always had him on my list as a member of the Vitezovi. There was Miso Mijic, Colonel, SIS, Vitezovi.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: You saw the document that I presented to you yesterday, according to which Miso Mijic appointed Darko Kraljevic as his deputy in the SIS, which means that one could be at the same time a member of the SIS and of the Vitezovi.

utterances.speaker: ANTE BRELJAS [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes. And there were others who were also in the SIS and in the Vitezovi. He was not the only one.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Mr. Breljas, do you make a distinction between what we call the administrative chain of command and the operational chain of command in all military units?

utterances.speaker: ANTE BRELJAS [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Certainly. Of course there is a vast difference.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that, administratively, one can depend on Mostar and to be under the command in Vitez of the sector when a military operation is involved?

utterances.speaker: ANTE BRELJAS [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes. Certainly. Of course. That is how things work, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Thank you. You were shown some documents this morning, the same ones I used yesterday. I should like us to go back to one of them, document Z808. It is the list drawn up by Mr. Zvonimir Cilic, the propaganda officer of the Vitez Brigade. Z808. Do you have this document now?

utterances.speaker: ANTE BRELJAS [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Yes, I have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Could you please look at page 2 and tell us what is the name under number 45?

utterances.speaker: ANTE BRELJAS [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Mile Vinac.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: And this person was apparently wounded during the conflict and as a member of the Vitez Brigade. We agree, don't we?

utterances.speaker: ANTE BRELJAS [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Thank you. I should now like to ask you to look at another document which was also shown to you this morning again, Z1279. It is a document dated 31st of October, 1993, drawn up by the defence administration. Could you please look at page 5 of this document, the point that was discussed already this morning. And at paragraph 6, measures taken by the administration. Do you see this paragraph?

utterances.speaker: ANTE BRELJAS [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: It is indicated, in the fourth line, that the defence administration of Vitez was placed under the provisional command of the Vitez Brigade. We agree on that, don't we?

utterances.speaker: ANTE BRELJAS [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: So when the Vitezovi received the order to bring conscripts back to the front, it was the Vitez Brigade that had responsibility over the defence office?

utterances.speaker: ANTE BRELJAS [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Thank you. Two final points of clarification.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Usher. We're finished with that document.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: This morning another document was discussed concerning people from Vitez television who were mobilised to the brigade, and reference was made to one cameraman during your cross-examination this morning.

utterances.speaker: ANTE BRELJAS [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: And in fact, in your statement and testimony yesterday you always spoke of two different people, two different persons, two cameramen.

utterances.speaker: ANTE BRELJAS [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: The one you identified as having accompanied you to Tisovac.

utterances.speaker: ANTE BRELJAS [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Stipovic, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Srecko Stipovic. You gave us his name and you recognised his name on the document. You identified him.

utterances.speaker: ANTE BRELJAS [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes. Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: He was not on the front on that day. He was with you at Tisovac.

utterances.speaker: ANTE BRELJAS [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes. That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: And then you also spoke of a second cameraman who was to film the judge, Poricanin.

utterances.speaker: ANTE BRELJAS [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes. That's quite a different man, whom I didn't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you know that Mr. Cerkez was born in Rijeka? That is where Kraljevic lived, the same place that Kraljevic lived in.

utterances.speaker: ANTE BRELJAS [RESUMED]
utterances.text: I know he was born someplace between the old station and the centre of the town. I know that it was in that area. Once somebody showed me Cerkez's house. That is what I heard from others. I didn't know, but I heard from others that Mario Cerkez's house was there. And then a logistics man of his lived right next to him. He had a house right next to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I have no further questions for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Lopez-Terres, could you help me with this: The Vitezovi, on some of these documents, are referred to as "PPN."

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What is the significance of the "PPN"?

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, of course I don't speak the Croatian language, but on the document shown to you as an exhibit, you have the definition. It is an abbreviation which means a special purpose unit, a special unit, task force. In English it has always been translated as a "special purpose unit."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Breljas, that concludes your evidence. You are now released. Thank you for coming to the International Tribunal to give your evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: While the witness is leaving, we were handed various statements which he had made. Mr. Stein, yesterday, said he didn't want them exhibited. Unless anybody else wants them exhibited, I shall hand them back. Mr. Nice, we've been given the summary of Mr. Beese. Unless you propose to call him or ask to call him next week, we've been given a broad indication about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'll delay the calling of him for a couple of weeks now, but may the summary stay with you. I know that sometimes it's helpful to have the summaries in advance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Indeed, I'm going to have served on you the summary of (redacted), who I had some hopes I might be able to call tomorrow, but I'm not pretty well certain I won't be able to call tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. It may be convenient if I deal with our decision about the programme for next week.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. And just before you do it, in case it should have any bearing on it, I think that the remaining evidence available, assuming I can't whistle up (redacted) by telephone call now for tomorrow, the remaining evidence, I think, will go into tomorrow, but probably only just. I haven't checked with Mr. Scott, who is calling the next witness, how long he expects to be, but the third witness whom I'm going to call and whose summary I will serve at the end of this break will be very short indeed. I think we'll just go into tomorrow. It would be nice to get (redacted) over here, but although I contacted him last week and had the number, he's not responding to the phone number at the moment. So I'm not hopeful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Dealing with the programme for next week, the issue arises whether we, as two Judges, should hear the evidence under Rule 15 bis. Mr. Stein, on behalf of the Defence, raised the objection or the concern that Judge Robinson would have much extra material to read. I've taken the opportunity of speaking to the Judge on the telephone in Jamaica. I passed on the condolences which were expressed in Court yesterday. I told him of the concerns mentioned about his having a lot of material to read, extra material. He did not regard this as a source of any difficulty, and he would be well able to read the extra pages of transcript. In our judgement, therefore, this deals with those concerns and objections. That being so, we have to consider whether it is in the interests of justice, under Rule 15 bis, for us to sit next week. Given the length of time which this case has taken already and is likely to take, and our duty to pursue the matter expeditiously, we consider that it is in the interests of justice to hear the evidence next week, sitting as two Judges for three days, and we consider it appropriate to apply the Rule. Accordingly, we will sit next week for three days, Monday to Wednesday, to hear evidence. Thursday we shall not hear evidence, but it appears that it may be convenient to have that time available for a Status Conference, to discuss any matters which may be outstanding, to hear what submissions we can. We can discuss that over the next few days. There is one additional matter about the future programme, and it is this: That Judge Robinson, in fact, will not be returning on Monday the 24th but will return on Tuesday the 25th. Accordingly, we shall not sit in this case on the morning, as it would be, of the 24th -- there was only the morning available that day -- but we will resume the hearings on the 25th. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That's very helpful, Your Honour. Next Thursday I think I shan't be here in the afternoon, but in any event, it looks as though the Status Conference will be likely to take place in the morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, it certainly would. Very well. We'll adjourn now. Half an hour. 11.35.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: May the witness come in, but just before he does, (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Scott, with more efficiency, will take the next witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, let the witness take the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Would you like to take a seat.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Your Honour, it may be that everyone in the Court already knows this, but Colonel de Boer -- in my opinion, he speaks quite good English -- prefers for these official purposes to speak in Dutch. So we may have an additional layer of translation to deal with. Colonel de Boer, first of all, is your full name Johannes Jacobus de Boer?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES JACOBUS DE BOER
utterances.text: I am waiting for the interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: My understanding is there was going to be a Dutch interpreter in the French booth, if I'm correct.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: But from Dutch, Mr. Scott, not into Dutch.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What's the position?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, I apologise for the difficulty. It appears that, if it's okay with the witness, I put my questions -- if I understand correctly where we are, I can ask my questions in English, he can give his answers in Dutch, and his answers will then be interpreted for the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The interpretation is only one way, in Dutch to English?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: That's what I am hearing, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, Colonel, I hope we can get on like that.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I am reminded to speak in the microphone. I hope we can get on. I don't see that we are doing very well so far. Let's start again.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour. I thought it was all arranged. My apologies.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Colonel, then, if at any time you don't understand my English question, or if I am speaking too fast, please alert me to that. Colonel, is it correct then that your full name is Johannes Jacobus de Boer?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES JACOBUS DE BOER
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You are presently a colonel in the Dutch Army, assigned at the Nederlands Defence College; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES JACOBUS DE BOER
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: During the time, including November 1992 to May 1993, Colonel, you were a lieutenant-colonel serving as the commander of the 105th Dutch Transportation Battalion; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES JACOBUS DE BOER
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And from approximately November of 1992 to 3rd of May, 1993, you acted as the commander of the 1st U.N., or perhaps UNPROFOR Transportation Battalion, located or based in Busovaca; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES JACOBUS DE BOER
utterances.text: It is correct in that sense that I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Can we have the interpretation, please?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES JACOBUS DE BOER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And I left the area on the 3rd of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I understand, sir, that before you arrived for your full tour of duty in Bosnia-Herzegovina, that in about July of '92 you visited on what might be called a reconnaissance mission to orient yourself to the area and prepare to move your unit into the area, and at that time you met the mayor of Vitez, a man named Ivan Santic. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES JACOBUS DE BOER
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let's clarify one point, please. In your statement from 1995 you referred to having dealings with a man named Skopljak. You recall that?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES JACOBUS DE BOER
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Were you certain, or have you always been certain that the person you dealt with, in fact, was the mayor of Vitez?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES JACOBUS DE BOER
utterances.text: I was certain that it was the mayor of Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And on further recollection, have you in fact remembered that the mayor of Vitez, in fact, was Ivan Santic and not Mr. Skopljak?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES JACOBUS DE BOER
utterances.text: I do not really remember the name meaning that the mayor or, rather, the man I spoke to, introduced himself as the mayor of Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Very well. Let's move forward. Can you relate to the Court a particular conversation you had with the mayor of Vitez when you first arrived on this reconnaissance mission in Bosnia in about July 1992? And I don't want to get too much detail on this, but can you relate to the Court any conversation you had with him about a particular ethnic group?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES JACOBUS DE BOER
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Please do.

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES JACOBUS DE BOER
utterances.text: Yes. During the conversation which I had with the mayor, he said -- he stated that the Muslim part of the Vitez population behaved hygienically, that they were much below, much inferior to the rest of the population.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And what was your reaction, sir, to Mr. Santic stating this to you?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES JACOBUS DE BOER
utterances.text: I was taken aback, but I did not react to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Is it correct, sir, that after this first meeting with Mr. Santic, the mayor of Vitez, that you in fact, during your tour in Bosnia, had other meetings or dealings with Mr. Santic from time to time?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES JACOBUS DE BOER
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Is it correct, sir, that on one occasion toward the end of your time in Bosnia, that is about in the latter half of April 1993, is it correct that you went to the Vitez town hall looking for Mr. Santic, you saw HVO soldiers outside the building, a 20-millimetre cannon located in front of the entrance to the building, and you looked for Mr. Santic and found him in the basement of the building?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES JACOBUS DE BOER
utterances.text: Yes. That is quite correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, my continuing apologies. Mr. Nice suggested that it would be better if he didn't listen to his earphones in terms of the English translation. It may be more confusing. I'm not sure if that's the case, but it's coming from the interpreters. I'm in the witness's hands as to what's easiest for him, but I --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: May we explain the slight delay, because the interpretation is going into French and from French into English. That is why there's a delay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: There's bound to be a delay. Let us take things slowly but accurately, and particularly to make sure the witness feels entirely comfortable with the way things are being done.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Finishing on that topic or that item, sir, when you found Mr. Santic in the basement of the Vitez town hall, he said something to you around this time that the conflict between the Croats and Muslims had intensified; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES JACOBUS DE BOER
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: It is also correct that shortly after you arrived in Bosnia, sir, you met another individual named Zoran Maric, who you understood to be the mayor of Busovaca, who at that time was wearing civilian clothes?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES JACOBUS DE BOER
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did you, during your time in Bosnia, meet a man named Dario Kordic?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES JACOBUS DE BOER
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did you meet -- I'm not going to lead here, other than to point you to a particular date. Did you first meet Mr. Kordic around Christmas of 1992?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES JACOBUS DE BOER
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you relate to the court, please, in your own words --

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES JACOBUS DE BOER
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sorry. Can you relate to the Court, please, in your own words, your interaction with Mr. Kordic at that time? Can you tell the Court how Mr. Kordic was introduced to you and the basic thrust of your conversation?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES JACOBUS DE BOER
utterances.text: Sometime before Christmas 1992, I organised a reception, I gave a reception in Busovaca, in my headquarters. I met both the civilian and military authorities of both sides, Bosnian Croats; that is, Croats from Bosnia and Muslims from Bosnia, and we met on the occasion of Christmas. I had invited both parties on purpose, in order to show that my battalion was an independent unit, and civilian and military authorities were present from both sides, and even the Muslim side were also represented by religious authorities. Mr. Kordic was introduced to me by my interpreter as Colonel Kordic.
